title: Operating Prometheus Itself
intro: Monitoring is only useful if the monitoring system is healthy. Validating config before reloading, and inspecting scrape targets, keeps you from silently losing visibility.

steps.prompt: You edited prometheus.yml to add a new scrape job. Validate it before applying.
steps.fake_output:
Checking prometheus.yml
  SUCCESS: 2 rule files found
 SUCCESS: prometheus.yml is valid prometheus config file syntax
steps.explanation: Syntax and semantics are both valid.
steps.why: A broken config plus a reload can leave Prometheus refusing the new config — or, on restart, not starting at all. Validation first is the equivalent of 'nginx -t' before reload.

steps.prompt: Tell the running Prometheus to reload its configuration without restarting.
steps.explanation: The new config takes effect; in-memory data and scrape state are preserved.
steps.why: This endpoint only works if Prometheus runs with --web.enable-lifecycle. A full restart works too, but loses the in-memory head block briefly and causes a gap in recent data.

steps.prompt: Check the health of every scrape target, including the last error for any that are failing.
steps.explanation: lastError gives the exact reason: an i/o timeout reaching web02:9100.
steps.why: 'up == 0' tells you a target is down; this tells you WHY. A timeout points at a firewall (see networking-incident-005), while 'connection refused' means the exporter isn't running.

steps.prompt: Query Prometheus's HTTP API directly for current memory availability — how dashboards and scripts get data.
steps.explanation: Any PromQL query can be run via /api/v1/query and returns JSON.
steps.why: Quote the whole URL in real shells — PromQL's braces, brackets, and quotes otherwise get mangled by the shell. /api/v1/query_range returns a time series over a window instead of a single point.
